Evidence: "Data for this analysis were obtained following the 2020 revision of the Uganda HIV Prevention, Care and Treatment Guidelines that recommended HIVDR testing for all children and adolescents living with HIV failing ART. In 2021, the Uganda Ministry of Health conducted standard-of-care HIVDR testing for CLHIV failing first-line ART to optimize treatment outcomes, through the support of the CDC-funded Faith-based Action for Scaling up Testing and Treatment for the Epidemic Response (FASTER) project. FASTER was implemented between 2019-2021 by Catholic Relief Services, in partnership with the Clinton Health Access Initiative, to support ministries of health in four countries (Uganda, Nigeria, Tanzania and Zambia) to improve testing and treatment of CLHIV. \(^{8}\)

Data for this analysis came from previously collected VL samples from children aged  \(\leq 15\)  years of age on first-line ART enrolled in any ART-accredited health facility in Uganda whose VL sample satisfied the following criteria: (1) sample tested for VL between January and November 2021, (2) sample type was plasma (3) VF defined as

VL ≥1000 copies/mL for children on EFV or NVP or repeat VL >1000 copies/ml for children on Lopinavir/ritonavir (LPV/r) or DTG. Repeat VL refers to a VL test taken after a child with an initial unsuppressed VL has undergone intensified adherence support for at least 3 months with 3 consecutive good adherence scores. Samples from CLHIV whose prior regimen changes were made for treatment simplification or due to policy changes and not VF were classified as being on first-line ART.

A paper-based VL and HIVDR request form completed at sample collection contained details such as demographics, ART history, clinical condition, sample type and collection date for each sample. At the time of this evaluation, all VL testing was done centrally at the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL). CPHL had an electronic VL laboratory information system (LIMS) where the details from the VL and HIVDR request form were entered along with VL testing results, once available. LIMS data were used to filter remnant VL samples eligible for HIVDR testing based on the above inclusion criteria.

The eligible VL samples were then automatically identified by the HIV Drug Resistance Database (HIVDR Database). The HIVDR Database acts as the relay database for cross-laboratory systems interoperability. The database received eligible sample profiles from the VL LIMS and provided a user interface for referring these samples to the HIVDR laboratories. Once a sample fulfilling the inclusion criteria above was identified, it was retrieved and sent to the HIVDR laboratory at Joint Clinical Research Centre to be tested using Sanger sequencing technology if there was sufficient sample volume. Once a sample was referred to the HIVDR laboratory, clinicians received email notifications from the HIVDR Database to upload their clients' social, psychosocial, and

medical profiles into the database. When the HIVDR results were available, the HIVDR laboratory systems automatically pushed the results into the HIVDR Database, from which clinicians and experts could review the results and make ART recommendations. Once individual treatment decisions were made and documented, these clinical recommendations were also uploaded into the HIVDR database.

The data presented in this work were therefore a combination of the routine data inputs by clinicians, VL and HIVDR laboratories, and drug resistance review committees, all aggregated within the HIVDR Database. These data were stored in a relational database and were extracted, cleaned, and transformed using the Structured Query Language and exported as a Comma Separated Value database for further cleaning and analysis.

The analytic dataset of demographic data and HIVDR information for sampled specimens were retrieved from the HIVDR Database in March 2022. HIV drug resistance mutations (DRMs) and drug susceptibility profiles were generated using Stanford University's HIVdb algorithm (version 9.0) (https://hivdb.stanford.edu/hivdb). All analyses were conducted using Stata 18 statistical software (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX). Frequencies of DRMs were calculated overall and stratified by drug class of the mutation, including mutations against NRTIs, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors (PIs), and integrase inhibitors (INSTIs). The frequencies of individual DRMs were also calculated overall and stratified by regimen at sample collection. Mutations and resistance were classified as non-NNRTI if they were identified in any of the following drug classes; NRTIs, PIs, and/or INSTIs. Individuals were considered to have clinically significant HIVDR if their drug susceptibility profile revealed intermediate-to-high level

drug resistance to one or more of the following individual ARVs: DTG, abacavir (ABC), zidovudine (AZT), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine (3TC), LPV/r, darunavir (DRV), EFV, or NVP. All calculations were estimated overall, and stratified by regimen at blood sample collection, and by previous exposure to the child's known historical treatment regimens.

To determine possible correlates of DRMs and HIVDR, associations with various demographic and clinical factors were determined using chi square tests. P-values  \(< 0.05\)  were considered statistically significant. The outcomes of interest were presence of any DRMs and presence of intermediate-to-high level drug resistance to any non-NNRTI ARVs. Demographic and clinical variables explored included sex, age category, duration of time on ART, reported level of adherence to ART (good, fair, or poor), VL category at sample collection (defined as VL  \(< 10,000\), VL 10,000-100,000, and VL>100,000), and regimen at sample collection. A standardized behavioral questionnaire was completed for participants as part of their clinical care; correlates of DRMs and drug susceptibility were also explored for a variety of social susceptibility factors. To better characterize children on optimized ART, demographic factors were described for children on DTG-based regimens by their specific NRTI backbone. Among these children, presence of DRMs and non-NNRTI drug resistance was compared between children on DTG+ABC regimens compared to other DTG-based regimens using chi square tests.

Frequencies were also calculated for the clinical recommendations reported after HIVDR testing, both overall and stratified by drug class of DRMs. The potential clinical recommendations included maintaining on current regimen, substituting with another

ARV within the first-line, switching to another drug class or second-line regimen, or pending if clinical recommendations were not noted.

This activity was reviewed by CDC, deemed not research, and was conducted consistent with applicable federal law and CDC policy. \(^{1}\)

## Results

Between January and November 2021, 648 VL samples from 164 sites met the inclusion criteria. A total of 428 (66.0%) samples were retrieved from the sample biorepository and sent to the HIVDR lab for testing; 128 (19.8%) did not meet the Sanger testing criteria due to low sample volume or other factors. Of the 428 samples referred for HIVDR testing, 333 (77.8%) samples were successfully tested while 95 (22.2%) samples failed to amplify.

Among the 333 CLHIV with successful sample amplification, 61 (18.3%) were aged 1-4 years, 79 (23.7%) aged 5-9 years, 89 (26.7%) aged 10-12 years, and 104 (31.2%) aged 13-15 years (Table 1). There were 101 (30.3%) CLHIV taking ART for less than five years, 104 (31.2%) taking ART 5-9 years, and 128 (38.4%) taking ART 10 or more years. At the time of sample collection, 122 (36.6%) CLHIV were taking a DTG-based regimen, 136 (40.8%) were taking an LPV/r-based regimen, and 74 (22.2%) were taking either an EFV- or NVP-based regimen. Among the 122 CLHIV on DTG-based regimens, the median age was 13 years (interquartile range [IQR]=11-14); 54 (44.2%) were on regimens with an ABC/3TC backbone, 65 (53.3%) had a TDF/3TC backbone, and 3

(2.5%) had an AZT/3TC backbone. The median age in years for these subgroups was 12 for ABC (IQR=10-13), 13 for TDF (IQR=12-14), and 9 for AZT (IQR=2-10).

Of the 333 CLHIV, 271 (81.4%) had any DRMs (Table 2); 10 (3.0%) had any INSTI DRMs; 39 (11.7%) had any PI DRMs; 217 (65.2%) had any NRTI DRMs; and 225 (67.6%) had any NNRTI DRMs. Many CLHIV had DRMs against multiple classes of ARTs: 184 (55.3%) had DRMs against 2 classes and 36 (10.8%) had DRMs against 3 classes. These frequencies varied by regimen at sample collection (Table 2) and history of ARV exposure (Table 3). Of note, children on DTG at sample collection had lower frequencies of DRMs for all drug classes except INSTIs. Rates of DRMs against INSTIs among children on DTG were low (6.6%, 8/122), though were twice as common in these children when compared to the overall sample (3.0%, 10/333) and about 6 times more common when compared to CLHIV not on DTG at sample collection (0.95%, 10/333). The most common individual DRMs are presented in Table 4. The top 12 most common DRMs were NRTI or NNRTI mutations; 203 (61.0%) CLHIV had the most common NRTI mutation (M184V), and 143 (42.9%) had the most common NNRTI mutation (K103N). The two most common PI mutations were each found in 23 (6.9%) CLHIV (M46, V82) and 4 (1.2%) CLHIV had the most common INSTI mutation (R263).

Drug susceptibility analysis revealed that the majority of CLHIV (78.7%, 262/333) had clinically significant resistance (intermediate-to-high level drug resistance) to at least one ARV, including: DTG (1.8%), LPV (9.6%), DRV (1.8%), NVP (67.0%), EFV (66.1%), 3TC (61.0%), ABC (25.5%), and AZT (19.2%) (Table 2). Similar to DRMs, individual drug susceptibility varied by regimen at sample collection (Table 2) and history of ARV exposure (Table 3). CLHIV on DTG-based regimens at the time of sample collection

had the lowest prevalence of any intermediate-to-high level drug resistance at  \(69.7\%\), with resistance to EFV (58.2%) and NVP (59.8%) most frequent (Table 2). Of the 122 CLHIV failing on DTG, intermediate-to-high-level resistance was lower for other ARVs, including for: DTG (4.1%), LPV (4.1%), DRV (0.8%), ABC (21.3%), AZT (18%), and TDF (6.6%) (Table 2). Among 136 children failing on LPV/r, intermediate-to-high level resistance included: LPV/r (14.0%), DTG (0.7%), DRV (1.5%), ABC (27.2%), AZT (14.0%), and TDF (8.8%) (Table 2). All those with AZT resistance were also resistant to ABC leaving only 18 (13.2%) of those failing LPV/r with intermediate-high level ABC resistance and without similar AZT resistance. On average, intermediate-to-high level resistance to a particular drug tended to be higher in CLHIV on a regimen containing that drug at sample collection compared to the level of resistance to that drug among all sampled CLHIV. For instance, resistance to DTG was approximately eight times as high among CLHIV currently taking DTG (4.1%) compared to CLHIV not taking DTG (0.5%) [chi squared  \(p = 0.02\) ] and approximately 2 times higher to AZT (32.1% compared to 16.8%,  \(p = 0.01\) ) and LPV (14.0% compared to 6.6%,  \(p = 0.02\) ) for those on regimens containing these drugs, respectively. However, notably, this pattern was not seen for ABC (Table 2).

In bivariate analyses, similar patterns were seen for presence of DRMs and presence of non-NNRTI intermediate-to-high level drug resistance (Table 5). Overall, the youngest CLHIV were more likely to have DRMs  \((p = 0.02)\)  and were more likely to have any non-NNRTI resistance  \((p = 0.01)\). CLHIV on DTG-based regimens at sample collection were less likely to have both DRMs  \((p = 0.007)\)  or non-NNRTI resistance  \((p = 0.02)\)  compared to those on non-DTG-based regimens, and CLHIV on LPV/r-based regimens were more

likely to have both DRMs  \((p = 0.04)\)  and non-NNRTI resistance  \((p = 0.05)\)  compared to those on non-LPV/r-based regimens. Among CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen at sample collection, the 54 (44.3%) children with an ABC-containing backbone were no more likely to have clinically relevant mutations  \((p = 0.9)\)  or non-NNRTI resistance  \((p = 0.5)\)  compared to children on a DTG-based regimen with a different backbone. No relationship was seen for either DRMs or intermediate-to-high level resistance by sex, duration on ART, adherence score, VL at sample collection (Table 5), or most social susceptibility factors (Table S1).

At the time of data collection, almost half of CLHIV in the database (N=145, 43%) had no information on clinical recommendations after HIVDR testing (Table S2). However, among those with clinical recommendations, 94 (28.2%) were maintained on their current regimen, 55 (16.5%) were switched to another drug class, and 39 (11.7%) had a single drug substitution.

## Discussion:

This analysis demonstrated low levels of INSTI and PI HIVDR among Ugandan CLHIV experiencing VF on first-line ART and represents the largest examination of HIVDR among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens in Sub-Saharan Africa to date. While overall rates of DRMs were high, the majority of DRMs were to NNRTIs with low rates to INSTIs and PIs. We found that CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen were least likely to have any DRMs (including non-NNRTI DRMs) compared to all other regimens, with  \(>95\%\)  susceptible to DTG, LPV/r, and DRV/r. The finding of limited DTG resistance amongst children failing on DTG indicates that most children could be maintained on

their DTG-based ART with more emphasis on intensified, effective adherence support to help them achieve VS. Low rates of DRV/r resistance further support the use of DRV as an effective second-line ARV, even amongst those CLHIV failing on LPV/r. We also found that the prevalence of intermediate-to-high level resistance to ABC and AZT was relatively low ( \(\leq 25\%\) ) and was similar across all CLHIV, regardless of regimen at sample collection, suggesting the preferred maintenance of an ABC backbone for CLHIV  \(< 30\mathrm{kg}\)  when transitioning to a DTG-based regimen despite virologic failure.

Consistent with existing literature is the finding that the majority (81.4%) of CLHIV with VF have at least one DRM, with a similar prevalence of NNRTI (67.6%) and NRTI (65.2%) DRMs and the most common mutations seen by class were K103N and M184V, respectively. \(^{7,9-11}\)  Consistent with emerging literature is the finding that the proportion of CLHIV with NNRTI DRMs does not vary between those on a PI- or NNRTI-based regimen, \(^{12}\)  although this study found lower rates of NNRTI DRMs among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. Our results also showed lower rates of clinically significant resistance to 3TC among those on DTG compared to those on LPV/r, which is consistent with a small but growing body of research that suggests DTG-based regimens may be associated with lower rates of emerging HIVDR. \(^{13,14}\)  Similar to other smaller HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens, we saw low rates of INSTI DRMs (6.6% in our study, range 5.8-18% in other studies) and even lower rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DTG (4.1% in our study, range 8.9%-18% in other studies). \(^{14-16}\)  Though analysis methodologies differ across prior studies due to

differences in the sample population, ART at sample collection, and sampling approaches, all findings continue to demonstrate DTG efficacy and support DTG-based regimens as preferred first-line among CLHIV.

The novel findings in our study included the relatively large number of CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen with a WHO-recommended ABC+3TC backbone for CLHIV  \(< 30\mathrm{kg}\)  compared to other HIVDR studies among CLHIV on DTG-based regimens. \(^{14,15,17}\)  While results from the NADIA trial have demonstrated the durability and non-inferiority of DTG when paired with a 3TC +TDF backbone even when no NRTI activity is predicted, questions remain as to whether these findings apply to CLHIV, especially those who would be optimized to DTG using a single drug substitution while maintaining their ABC+3TC backbone. \(^{18}\)  Our findings demonstrate that among this highly treatment experienced population of CLHIV, those with a DTG+ABC containing regimen were no more likely to have DRMs or intermediate-to-high level non-NNRTI resistance than those on DTG with a non-ABC containing backbone. Additionally, similar rates of clinically significant resistance to ABC and AZT were seen among CLHIV on a DTG-based regimen, despite higher known exposure to ABC than AZT and few children currently on AZT. While further data are needed, our findings also support the maintenance of an ABC-containing backbone among children failing LPV/r-based regimens, as we demonstrated that only  \(13.2\%\)  of our population failing LPV/r may potentially benefit from switching to an AZT-containing backbone. The low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to TDF seen in both CLHIV on DTG and LPV/r along with results from the NADIA trial, underscore the importance of transitioning all CLHIV on DTG to a TDF-containing regimen once they reach  \(30\mathrm{kg}\), such as

Tenofovir/Lamivudine/Dolutegravir (TLD), which has been shown to improve VS regardless of underlying NRTI resistance.

Our study found higher rates of LPV/r resistance than previously reported among children on LPV/r-based regimens. Our findings of  \(14\%\)  intermediate-to-high level resistance to LPV/r were slightly higher than the 1-10.7% reported in other studies. \(^{12,15,19}\)  However, our study also contributes to a small but increasingly important body of evidence which demonstrates very low rates of intermediate-to-high level resistance to DRV/r amongst children on LPV/r and DTG, indicating that DRV may be the more promising PI for second-line regimens, even in the presence of LPV/r resistance. \(^{12,15,19}\)

Consistent with limited available data, our study found that younger children (<5 years old) are more likely to have DRMs and intermediate-to-high level resistance. \(^{7,19}\)  This has important clinical implications, as these young children will need ART throughout their lives, and it will be important to prevent additional development of resistance to currently available, optimal regimens. Sample size limited our ability to further analyze resistance by regimen in these young children, but this would be an important focus of future HIVDR surveys. This analysis took place before full introduction of DTG 10mg in Uganda so further investigation into this age band is warranted as most CLHIV  \(<5\)  years will have now fully transitioned to DTG.

At the time of this analysis only  \(56.5\%\)  (188/333) of CLHIV had a clinical outcome reported in their chart. Half of those with a reported outcome were maintained on their current regimen. These data suggest moderate durability of current regimens despite

high levels of HIVDR; however, minimal clinical outcome data limited our ability to draw meaningful conclusions about the impact of HIVDR testing on clinical outcomes.

An important strength of this analysis is that it is one of the first to result from HIVDR testing conducted as part of standard of care HIV treatment for all CLHIV. However, there were also several limitations, including those originating from identified gaps in programmatic HIVDR testing. Primarily, samples were only obtained from those CLHIV on ART who returned for follow up VL testing, none of whom were eligible CLHIV 16-19 years and only about half of the samples identified as eligible for inclusion were successfully traced, processed, and amplified. This limits the study's full

representativeness of the population and prevents interpretation for older adolescents.

To improve data quality in the future, improvements can be made in tracing and processing for samples eligible for HIVDR testing, as well as to better understand the factors that contributed to unsuccessful amplification for a number of the samples.

These challenges and resulting lower sample size consequently limited our ability to perform more robust analyses between and within treatment groups. Additionally, due to delays in HIVDR turnaround time and review of clinical HIVDR results, as well as gaps in documentation of clinical management using HIVDR results, we had limited ability to analyze treatment decisions' outcomes and therefore could not robustly evaluate the clinical impact of standard of care HIVDR testing. Further evaluations will be important once measures to improve turnaround time and documentation are implemented.

In conclusion, among this cohort of Ugandan CLHIV failing their first-line ART regimen, the findings of low rates of INSTI mutations and overall lower rates of clinically significant HIVDR among those on a DTG-based regimen underscores the durability of

DTG-based regimens, highlighting the importance of a rapid transition to DTG-based ART for all CLHIV, and the value of effective adherence support for those CLHIV on DTG with VF. The rates of cross-resistance seen between ABC and AZT, regardless of ART backbone at sample collection, support maintaining an ABC backbone for CLHIV  \(< 30\)  kg, at the time of DTG transition even without VL results. Further data on clinical outcomes of CLHIV with VF maintained on DTG-based regimens, especially in the presence of NRTI and INSTI resistance, could better inform guidance on the timing and necessity of a switch to a second-line regimen.

What method was used for sequencing?

Evidence: "HIVDR testing in Uganda All PLHIV on ART in Uganda receive a VL test annually. Those with a non-suppressed VL undergo intensive adherence counselling (IAC) for three months with a repeat VL at the end. Individuals with a persistent non- suppressed VL are eligible for an HIVDR test. A Plasma or dried blood spot (DBS) sample is collected and referred to the HIVDR testing facility at a central national laboratory. Here, RNA extraction is done using commercial kits followed by reverse transcription and Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) amplification. PCR is a molecular technique used to amplify specific DNA sequences by generating millions of copies from a small initial sample. This step is crucial for increasing the quantity of genetic material required for sequencing. Sequencing, where individual mutations are identified using either Sanger sequencing or Next generation sequencing is then carried out. Mutations are identified and interpreted using the Stanford HIV drug resistance database [18-20]. The results of the HIVDR test are uploaded onto the national database together with the patients clinical and demographic information."

Rationale: The evidence mentions that the HIVDR testing in Uganda involves RNA extraction, reverse transcription, and PCR amplification, followed by sequencing. It does not specify the type of sequencing method used, but it mentions that mutations are identified using either Sanger sequencing or Next generation sequencing.
